Annular multipliers and elliptic endpoints

Exposition and original illustrations by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Public domain (CC0 1.0).

A multiplier can be controlled by averaged derivatives on each frequency annulus. Its inverse kernels need not satisfy a pointwise gradient estimate away from the origin: integrable translation differences and integrable tails are enough. Cancellation inside cubes then gives the weak first endpoint, all finite intermediate exponents and Hölder continuity. Applied to a reciprocal elliptic polynomial, these bounds recover the derivatives of a distributional solution. At the continuous endpoint an explicit sum of shrinking annuli shows why the conclusion changes.

Use , with coefficient , , and . The complete Fourier maps and their distributional agreement are proved in Fourier–Laplace slices and boundary poles, Lemma 0.1. Fractional energy and sharp Fourier embeddings, Lemma 1 and Corollary 6, gives the integer Sobolev norm, reciprocal pairing and continuous embedding. The Schwartz Fourier foundation, F1–F5, supplies inversion and all test-space identities.

The cube decomposition used below is the complete proof of Lemma 6.1 in Convolution estimates and weak-gradient embeddings. The integration foundation, §§15–16, proves Hölder, Young, Tonelli, dominated convergence, completeness and smooth approximation. Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3 and Theorem 1.1, gives compact-factor convolution, finite-order parameter pairings and derivative transfer. Tempered growth and spectral cutoffs, Lemma 2.1, proves convolution with a Schwartz factor and its Fourier identity. Scalar differentiation, compact cutoffs and finite Taylor formulas are in the scalar foundation, §13. The angular foundation, A4, supplies polar integration.

Elliptic equations with arbitrary distributional input

A constant-coefficient polynomial of degree is elliptic if its principal homogeneous part has no zero on the real unit sphere. Complex coefficients are allowed.

The full multiplier still acts inside the cube and in its estimate. A kernel description valid only off the origin would not determine this diagonal contribution.
